query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with controlled short-range chemical ordering form a stable, coherent passivating oxide layer (rich in elements such as Al and Cr) during high-temperature oxidation that concurrently preserves their mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, while maintaining low density. In contrast, alloys lacking such ordering will demonstrate faster oxidation kinetics, diminished mechanical integrity, and inferior corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Lightweight high-entropy alloy processed to exhibit defined short-range chemical ordering versus a baseline alloy processed with minimal ordering.
generation.intervention: Perform real-time in situ oxidation and corrosion monitoring (e.g., using high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron techniques) comparing the short-range ordered HEA to a baseline alloy (minimal ordering) under identical thermal and corrosive conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (e.g., around 900 °C or service-relevant temperatures for aerospace/rail applications) in oxidizing and corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to air with traces of water vapor or salt solutions), with testing limited to temperatures where the ordering remains stable. The hypothesis is expected to cease holding if temperatures exceed the stability range of the short-range order or if prolonged exposure leads to its degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering at the atomic level that promotes the formation and maintenance of a coherent protective oxide/passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: The prearranged local chemical order acts as a diffusion barrier that slows the outward diffusion of reactive elements and the inward ingress of oxygen, thereby enabling the formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3-based passivation layer. This stable oxide film mitigates oxidation damage and curtails corrosion while helping retain the mechanical strength of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ characterization should reveal that the short-range ordered HEA forms a more uniform and continuous oxide layer with slower oxidation kinetics, and mechanical testing should show less deterioration in strength and corrosion resistance compared to the baseline alloy lacking such ordering.
generation.baseline: Baseline lightweight HEA with similar elemental composition but minimal short-range chemical ordering.
generation.boundary: The protective synergy is expected to fail if the operating temperature surpasses the stability limit of the short-range ordering (leading to ordering breakdown) or if the alloy is subjected to extreme corrosive conditions that overwhelm the passivation effect.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds for ordering stability and the precise contribution of short-range order to the diffusion barrier remain uncertain, and the interplay may vary with minor compositional adjustments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of lightweight HEAs – one processed to achieve controlled short-range chemical ordering and one processed to minimize such ordering. Subject both alloys to identical high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 900 °C in air) and corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) while performing in situ TEM and synchrotron measurements to monitor oxide layer formation, phase evolution, and microstructural changes. Conduct periodic mechanical tests (e.g., hardness and tensile strength) before, during, and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide layer continuity and composition (via in situ TEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA variant with controlled short-range ordering does not show statistically significant improvements in oxide layer uniformity/stability, slower oxidation kinetics, and better retention of mechanical and corrosion properties compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that short-range ordering mediates the combined property synergy is falsified.

Previous studies have demonstrated that inert anodes used in aluminum electrolysis, made from medium-entropy alloys (Fe-Ni-Cu), exhibit excellent high-temperature stability and corrosion resistance. These alloys form a protective NiFe2O4 layer at elevated temperatures, significantly improving their corrosion resistance [,]. Cr primarily improves the alloy’s corrosion resistance and oxidation resistance by forming a stable protective oxide layer. Co enhances the high-temperature stability of the alloy and increases its strength, making it suitable for high-stress and high-temperature environments. In this study, the oxidation behavior of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated in air at 900 °C, and their corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl solution was evaluated using potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The following conclusions were drawn:(1)The oxidation kinetics of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs in air at 900 °C follow a parabolic relationship. Among them, the FeNiCuAlCr HEA exhibited excellent oxidation resistance, with a low mass gain of 0.83 mg/cm2 after 108 h of exposure at 900 °C.(2)The outer oxidation layer of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA formed a dense and continuous Al2O3 and Cr2O3 layer, which provided effective protection for the substrate. decision.trend: Beginning with Ti–Al–Cr–Nb–V medium-entropy alloys (PMC9506522) that highlighted low density (~5 g/cm³) and enhanced mechanical strength via Zr additions, subsequent studies turned to Al- and Ti-based compositions for both mechanical and corrosion benefits. AlTiVNb thin films (PMC9735962) demonstrated high strength and ductility alongside significant corrosion resistance, and AlCrTiV0.5Cux systems (PMC10095625) offered similarly lightweight, corrosion-resistant solutions. More recently, a single-phase Al-based complex concentrated alloy (PMC11330973) delivered extraordinarily high specific strength at lower densities. Yet, none fully reconciled how to maintain ballistic-grade strength, aqueous durability, and high-temperature oxidation resistance simultaneously, leaving a key gap in understanding the underlying mechanisms that enable (or inhibit) the full property synergy.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how these alloys can form and sustain protective surface layers under both corrosive and high-temperature oxidative conditions, while retaining low density and mechanical strength. Specifically, the fundamental mechanism—whether it involves short-range chemical ordering, sluggish diffusion, stable passivation, or a combination thereof—requires clearer elucidation and direct experimental verification under relevant service conditions.
decision.lever: Perform real-time in situ oxidation and corrosion monitoring (e.g., with high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron techniques) on carefully processed lightweight high-entropy alloys that have controlled short-range chemical ordering. Compare these to a baseline alloy with minimal ordering, under the same composition and thermal exposures, to track how oxide and passivation layers form and how mechanical properties evolve. Characterize phase stability, oxidation/corrosion kinetics, and mechanical response in situ.
decision.why: Directly observing oxide-layer formation and changes in microstructure under service-relevant thermal and corrosive environments will clarify the mechanistic basis for the simultaneous retention or loss of strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation protection in lightweight high-entropy alloys. By probing structural, chemical, and mechanical changes in real time, we can identify the breaking point of the hypothesized synergy—namely, whether the loss of short-range order or the breakdown of stable passivation at high temperature leads to poor oxidation resistance and reduced mechanical performance.
